body:
Location and Foundation

Vikramashila, also written Vikramshila, was a major Buddhist centre of higher learning in eastern India. Its remains are located at Antichak, near Kahalgaon in Bhagalpur district, Bihar, close to the Ganga.

Vikramashila developed during the Pala period. Its foundation is traditionally attributed to Dharmapala, a ruler of the Pala dynasty, around the late 8th to early 9th century CE.

This distinguishes Vikramashila from Nalanda, which had already become prominent under the Guptas several centuries earlier.

Founder-location pair: Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty and was situated in present-day Bhagalpur district, Bihar.

Why Vikramashila Became Important

The Pala rulers were important patrons of Buddhist monasteries and centres of learning in eastern India. Their support helped institutions such as Nalanda and Vikramashila develop into centres of advanced teaching.

Vikramashila became especially associated with Vajrayana or Tantric Buddhist learning. Vajrayana refers to a tradition of Buddhism that includes particular ritual and contemplative practices alongside philosophical study.

However, Vikramashila's academic activity was not limited to ritual instruction. It was also known for broader scholarly learning.

Principal Fields of Study

The subjects associated with Vikramashila included:

  • Buddhist philosophy: advanced study of Buddhist doctrines and interpretation.
  • Logic: reasoning and the examination of philosophical arguments.
  • Grammar: precise understanding of language and scholarly texts.
  • Metaphysics: philosophical questions concerning existence and reality.
  • Vajrayana or Tantric studies: specialised Buddhist teachings and practices.

Vikramashila also contributed to the wider transmission of Buddhist scholarship, particularly through intellectual connections with Tibet.

Vikramashila and Nalanda

Both Nalanda and Vikramashila were important Buddhist centres in Bihar and received support from the Pala rulers. Their connection to the same dynasty does not mean they were founded at the same time.

Nalanda had developed centuries earlier, while Vikramashila was established under Dharmapala in the Pala period. The 2 institutions subsequently existed as major centres of Buddhist scholarship in eastern India.

Their subjects also overlapped, particularly in Buddhist philosophy, reasoning and language. Vikramashila is especially remembered for its association with Vajrayana Buddhism.

Prelims focus

  • Vikramashila was located at Antichak in Bhagalpur district, Bihar.
  • It was founded under the Pala ruler Dharmapala.
  • Its foundation belongs approximately to the late 8th or early 9th century CE.
  • It was a major Buddhist centre, especially associated with Vajrayana learning.
  • Its subjects included philosophy, logic, grammar and metaphysics.
  • Trap: Nalanda and Vikramashila were both supported by the Palas, but Nalanda was established earlier.

[Sources: Archaeological Survey of India, Patna Circle, 'Monuments Details', entry 'Ancient Site of Vikramshila Monastery, Antichak, Bhagalpur', consulted 18 November 2026; Bihar Tourism, 'Ruins of Vikramshila', location and historical description, consulted 18 November 2026; Bihar Tourism, Buddhist Circuit brochure, section 'Ruins of Vikramshila University', consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 72–73, 2024–25 reprint.]

body:
Why Foreign Travellers Matter

Foreign visitors recorded information about Indian rulers, religious institutions, towns and social practices. Their writings are useful because they describe aspects of life that the writers considered important or unfamiliar.

However, different visitors travelled for different purposes. A diplomatic representative who observed a royal court did not necessarily record the same subjects as a religious pilgrim seeking sacred texts.

Megasthenes and Faxian illustrate this distinction particularly clearly. They visited the subcontinent in different periods and produced different types of accounts.

Megasthenes: Greek Ambassador in the Mauryan Period

Megasthenes was a Greek diplomat associated with Seleucus I Nicator. He served as an ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya around the late 4th to early 3rd century BCE.

His account of India is known as the Indica. The complete original work has not survived; information from it is preserved through quotations and references in the writings of later authors.

What Megasthenes Recorded

Megasthenes described aspects of the Mauryan state and society. His account is particularly associated with:

  • Pataliputra: the major capital of the Mauryan Empire.
  • Administration: the activities of officials and arrangements for governing the empire.
  • Military organisation: arrangements for different branches of the army.
  • Society: descriptions of people and social groups.

One well-known passage describes a committee with 6 subcommittees responsible for aspects of military administration. They dealt with the navy, transport and supplies, infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants.

Megasthenes is therefore primarily remembered as an observer of the Mauryan court and administration, not as a Buddhist pilgrim or a student at Nalanda.

Faxian: Chinese Buddhist Pilgrim in the Gupta Age

Faxian, also written Fa Xian or Fa-Hien, was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled to India in the early 5th century CE.

His journey belongs to the Gupta period and is commonly associated with the reign of Chandragupta II. This ruler must not be confused with Chandragupta Maurya, who lived many centuries earlier.

Faxian left China in 399 CE and returned in approximately 413 CE. His account is generally known in English as A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms, translated from the Chinese title Foguo Ji.

Purpose and Observations

Faxian's principal purpose was to visit places associated with Buddhism and obtain reliable Buddhist manuscripts, particularly texts relating to monastic discipline.

His account contains information about:

  • Buddhist pilgrimage sites, monasteries and religious practices.
  • The condition of Buddhism in regions through which he travelled.
  • Some aspects of daily life and social conditions.
  • The practical difficulties of travelling across land and sea.

Faxian described certain communities treated as socially excluded and required to signal their presence in public places. This is an observation about social practices reported in his account, not evidence that every region followed an identical rule.

Faxian's Journey: Landward Travel and Return by Sea

Faxian travelled westward from China through Central Asia and entered the Indian subcontinent by land. After visiting Buddhist sites and collecting texts, he returned by a different route.

He departed by sea from Bengal, travelled through maritime routes that included Java, and eventually reached China.

The difficult voyage shows why the preservation and transmission of manuscripts mattered so much to Buddhist pilgrims. Their journeys helped carry Indian religious literature to other parts of Asia.

Distinguishing Their Accounts

Megasthenes and Faxian provide information about India, but they should be identified by period, purpose and work. Megasthenes belongs to the Mauryan period and wrote about the court and administration. Faxian belongs to the Gupta period and travelled primarily to study Buddhist religious life and collect scriptures.

Prelims focus

  • Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador to Chandragupta Maurya.
  • His work was Indica, which survives in fragments.
  • Megasthenes described Mauryan administration, including 6 military subcommittees.
  • Faxian was a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim of the early 5th century CE.
  • Faxian's work is known as A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.
  • Trap: Megasthenes is linked with Chandragupta Maurya; Faxian is associated with the Gupta age of Chandragupta II.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', sections 'Finding out about the Mauryas' and 'Administering the Empire', printed pp. 32–34; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims', printed pp. 105–106, 2018–19 edition; British Library, International Dunhuang Programme, 'Buddhist Travellers and Pilgrims', section 'Faxian', consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Faxian's return voyage carried Buddhist texts from India towards China.

title: Megasthenes and Faxian: Two Different Kinds of Foreign Accounts

body:
Chinese Pilgrims and Buddhist Scholarship

Buddhism spread from India to several parts of Asia. As Buddhist communities grew in China, monks sought opportunities to visit Indian pilgrimage sites, study with renowned teachers and obtain religious manuscripts.

Xuanzang and Yijing were 2 important Chinese Buddhist scholars who travelled to India in the 7th century CE. Both are closely associated with Nalanda, but their journeys and written accounts differ.

Xuanzang: Traveller During Harshavardhana's Reign

Xuanzang, also written Xuan Zang or Hiuen Tsang, travelled through India during the reign of Harshavardhana.

His journey extended approximately from 629 to 645 CE. He travelled by land through Central Asia and returned to China by an overland route.

His celebrated account is known as the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, also called the Da Tang Xiyu Ji.

What Xuanzang Recorded

Xuanzang described the regions he visited and supplied information about:

  • Buddhist institutions: monasteries, religious sites and centres of learning.
  • Nalanda: its teachers, educational standards and intellectual discussions.
  • Political conditions: important rulers and kingdoms, including Harshavardhana's realm.
  • Social and religious life: practices and conditions observed during his travels.

Xuanzang spent time at Harsha's court. His account therefore offers information about the political and religious life of northern India in the 7th century.

Xuanzang at Nalanda

Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in Bihar, where Shilabhadra was a distinguished teacher. Xuanzang studied Yogashastra and described the institution's learned teachers, discipline and demanding scholarly discussions.

He also visited Vallabhi in Gujarat and recorded information about its Buddhist establishments. He is therefore relevant to both Nalanda and Vallabhi.

Yijing: A Later Traveller Who Studied Monastic Practice

Yijing, also written I-Qing or I-Tsing, was another Chinese Buddhist monk. His major travels took place approximately between 671 and 695 CE, later than Xuanzang's journey.

Unlike Xuanzang, Yijing used the maritime route through Southeast Asia. His travels connected China, Southeast Asian Buddhist centres and India.

Yijing studied at Nalanda. He paid particular attention to the organisation of Buddhist religious life and the practices followed by monks.

What Yijing Recorded

Yijing is especially associated with accounts of:

  • Monastic discipline: the rules and duties of Buddhist monks.
  • Daily religious practices: worship, conduct and monastic routines.
  • Learning: the study of Buddhist texts and the education of monks.
  • Scholarly connections: the movement of Buddhist students and teachers between different Asian regions.

One of his important works is commonly translated as A Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago. He also wrote biographical accounts concerning Buddhist monks who travelled in search of religious learning.

Yijing identified Nalanda and Vallabhi as highly respected centres of Buddhist education. His discussion of Vallabhi demonstrates its reputation, although it should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of a personal visit there.

The Main Distinctions

Xuanzang is particularly useful for the description of regions, kingdoms, Buddhist sites and Nalanda's scholarly life. Yijing is especially useful for the detailed description of Buddhist monastic discipline, education and daily practices.

Their routes also differed. Xuanzang travelled overland, while Yijing used sea routes through Southeast Asia.

Prelims focus

  • Xuanzang travelled in India during the reign of Harshavardhana.
  • His account is the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.
  • Xuanzang studied at Nalanda under Shilabhadra.
  • Yijing travelled later in the 7th century and used maritime routes through Southeast Asia.
  • Yijing recorded Buddhist monastic practices and studied at Nalanda.
  • Trap: Xuanzang and Yijing were both Chinese Buddhist monks, but they did not make the same journey or write accounts with identical emphasis.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapters 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims' and 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 105–106 and 114, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 71–73, 2024–25 reprint; British Library, International Dunhuang Programme, 'Buddhist Travellers and Pilgrims', section 'Xuanzang', consulted 18 November 2026; 'Chinese Buddhist Travelers: Faxian, Xuanzang, and Yijing', Oxford Academic, account of travellers and routes, consulted 18 November 2026; Annette Schmiedchen, 'Maitrakas', Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, 2021.]

title: Xuanzang and Yijing: Chinese Pilgrims and India's Buddhist Universities
